778.title: Vana: exile
778.hook: Krishna comes to the forest, Draupadi tells him everything, and he explains why he wasn't there
778.carry: let them finish before you answer
778.howItsDone: Devotees revere Krishna as God, and storytellers dwell on this forest meeting, where Draupadi pours out her grief and Krishna promises that the wrongs done to her will be answered.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vana, the forest, where a vessel from the sun fed every guest, and Draupadi ate last. Your line was serve someone else first.

Chariots on a forest road. Word has reached Krishna's people that the Pandavas are in exile, and Krishna comes to find them, with kinsmen beside him. The cousins embrace. Then Draupadi speaks, and she doesn't make small talk. She tells him everything: the hall, being dragged in by her hair, the laughter, the husbands who sat silent. She weeps as she speaks. And under all of it is one question she doesn't quite need to say out loud. Where were you?
screen: `KRISHNA COMES TO THE FOREST.` → `DRAUPADI TELLS EVERYTHING.` → `WHERE WERE YOU?`

segments.voice: Notice what Draupadi does with her grief. She doesn't tidy it. She names each wrong, in order, to the one person she trusts to hear it whole. In the epic's telling, she even says she has no husband, no son, no friend, no brother, not even Krishna, because none of them protected her. That's a hard thing to say to someone's face. Krishna doesn't argue. He makes her a promise instead: the women of those who wronged her will one day weep as she is weeping now. Then, turning to Yudhishthira, he answers the question underneath. I wasn't there, he says. If I had been in Dvaraka, I would have come to that game uninvited and stopped it. But he was away, fighting a king named Shalva, who had attacked his city in a flying citadel. By the time he came home and heard, the dice had already fallen. It's a striking moment. Krishna, whom devotees worship as God, gives an account of his absence. He doesn't say the suffering was meant to happen. He doesn't tell Draupadi to be calm. He says, in effect: I was fighting somewhere else, and had I been home, I would have stopped it. Away from the palace and the hall, Draupadi says exactly what she thinks, even to Krishna, and he hears all of it before he answers.
screen: `DRAUPADI NAMES EACH WRONG.` · `KRISHNA MAKES A PROMISE.` · `I WAS FIGHTING SHALVA.` · then, large: `GRIEF SAID OUT LOUD, AND HEARD.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who once told you something hard, a hurt or a complaint, maybe even one about you, and remember how it felt to hear it. Now listen the way Krishna listens before he answers: breathe in and make room, breathe out and stay, no fixing, no defending. If you pray, bring that person into your prayer; if not, just hold them kindly in mind.

779.title: Vana: exile
779.hook: in the forest, Draupadi argues for anger and Yudhishthira argues for forgiveness, and the epic lets them both speak
779.carry: a time for strength, or to let go
779.howItsDone: Teachers and commentators return to this forest debate between Draupadi and Yudhishthira when discussing anger, forgiveness and right action, and Prahlada's answer to Bali is retold on its own as well.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vana, the forest, where Draupadi told Krishna everything, and he heard her to the end. Your line was let them finish before you answer.

An evening in the forest, and a married couple is having a real argument. Draupadi looks at her husband in his bark clothes, sleeping on the ground, and she can't stand it. You were a king, she says. Your brothers are suffering. How is your anger not blazing? Yudhishthira doesn't storm out. He answers her, at length. And she answers back. The epic doesn't cut the scene short or tell us who won. It gives both of them the floor.
screen: `A COUPLE ARGUES IN THE FOREST.` → `WHY IS YOUR ANGER NOT BLAZING?` → `BOTH OF THEM GET THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: Draupadi doesn't argue from feeling alone. She brings a story. Long ago, she says, the demon king Bali asked his grandfather Prahlada, the same Prahlada whose verdict Vidura told in the hall: which is better, forgiveness or might? Prahlada answered: neither one, always. Someone who forgives everything is treated with contempt, even by his own servants. Someone who never forgives makes enemies of everyone. There's a time for each, and wisdom is knowing which time it is. Now, says Draupadi, is the time for might. Yudhishthira answers with a different picture. Anger, he says, is the root of destruction. An angry person can't tell what should be said from what shouldn't, and will harm even those who deserve no harm. Forgiveness, in his telling, holds the world together; if no one forgave, there would be no peace among people at all. He calls forgiveness the strength of the strong. So who is right? Draupadi isn't the hothead, and Yudhishthira isn't the saint. Both quote the wisdom of their tradition. Both are suffering. Her point is about timing: forgiveness offered always can become weakness. His is about the self: anger acted on can burn the one who carries it. There's no court here, no audience of kings. Just two people who lost the same things, disagreeing honestly about what to do next.
screen: `PRAHLADA: A TIME FOR EACH.` · `DRAUPADI: NOW IS THE TIME FOR MIGHT.` · `YUDHISHTHIRA: ANGER DESTROYS.` · then, large: `BOTH QUOTE THEIR TRADITION.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing that still makes you angry, a medium one, not the biggest. Breathe in with Draupadi's question, is this a time for strength, and breathe out with Yudhishthira's, what would this anger do to me if I carried it. You don't need to settle the argument; if you pray, you can bring that situation into your prayer.

780.title: Vana: exile
780.hook: Bhima wants to fight now, and Yudhishthira holds to the word he gave in the hall
780.howItsDone: Yudhishthira's insistence on keeping his word in exile is held up in Hindu storytelling as a picture of satya, truthfulness, and is discussed alongside Bhima's very different temperament.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vana, the forest, and the great argument. Draupadi asked for might, Yudhishthira for forgiveness. Your line was a time for strength, or to let go.

Bhima has been listening, and he's done waiting. He's built for action, strong and impatient. He's watched his brothers live on roots and his wife sleep on the ground, and he can't see the point. Our enemies cheated, he says. Why are we keeping faith with cheats? Let's go back and take what's ours. It's a fair question, and he asks it loudly.
screen: `BHIMA IS DONE WAITING.` → `WHY KEEP FAITH WITH CHEATS?` → `THE BROTHER WHO GAVE HIS WORD.`

segments.voice: Bhima's case is strong, and the epic lets him make it in full. The game was a trap. Time is passing, and every day in the forest their enemies grow stronger. A warrior who sits still, he says, is failing at his own duty. Yudhishthira hears him out, then answers with one thing. I gave my word. In the hall, in front of everyone, he agreed to the terms of the last throw: the years in the forest, then a year in hiding. Breaking that promise now, he says, would be worse to him than losing the kingdom. The old word for what he's holding on to is satya: truth, and also truthfulness, being someone whose word holds. Then he adds something more practical, and more honest. Even if they wanted to fight now, look who stands on the other side: Bhishma, Drona, Karna, great warriors all. We aren't ready. So the forest isn't only a punishment to be endured. It's time: time to keep a promise, and time to prepare. Bhima's frustration isn't wrong, and the epic doesn't mock it. But Yudhishthira's refusal isn't weakness either. It's a man deciding that who he is matters more than how fast he gets his kingdom back. A stubborn sense of what he owes walked him back to the dice board when the old king summoned him. Here, it keeps four brothers and a wife waiting with him under the trees.
screen: `BHIMA: WHY WAIT?` · `YUDHISHTHIRA: I GAVE MY WORD.` · `SATYA: A WORD THAT HOLDS.` · then, large: `THE FOREST IS ALSO TIME.`

segments.voice: Think of a promise you're keeping that turned out harder than you expected: a commitment, a job, a way you said you'd treat someone. Let the Bhima in you ask, why not drop it, and breathe; then let the Yudhishthira in you ask, who would I be if I did, and breathe again. Nothing needs deciding now; if you pray, you can hold that promise in your prayer.

781.title: Vana: exile
781.hook: Vyasa walks into the forest camp with a plan: the waiting can become preparation, and Arjuna must go alone
781.carry: let the waiting become a plan
781.howItsDone: Retellings of the Mahabharata mark Vyasa's visit as the turn in the forest years, when Arjuna leaves to seek divine weapons; tradition names Vyasa as the epic's composer as well as a character in it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vana, the forest, where Bhima wanted to fight now, and Yudhishthira held to the word he gave. Your line was keep the word you gave.

An old sage walks into a stuck camp. Bhima wants them stronger, and soon. Yudhishthira won't break his word, and he knows how formidable the warriors on the other side are. The brothers are caught between impatience and patience. The visitor is Vyasa, grandfather of both the Pandavas and the Kauravas, and he has come with a way out.
screen: `STUCK BETWEEN IMPATIENCE AND PATIENCE.` → `VYASA WALKS IN.` → `WAITING BECOMES A PLAN.`

segments.voice: Vyasa takes Yudhishthira aside. I know what's in your heart, he says: the fear of Bhishma and Drona and Karna. So here's what to do. He gives Yudhishthira a sacred knowledge to teach to Arjuna, an inner discipline that will let him reach the gods. Arjuna must go, he says. He must seek out the gods themselves, Indra and Rudra and the guardians of the world, and win their weapons through ascetic effort. That is how the Pandavas will be ready when the time of exile ends. Now the argument looks different. Bhima wanted action, and here it is. Yudhishthira wanted to keep his word, and he does. Nobody breaks the terms; nobody leaves the forest early. But the waiting stops being empty. It becomes a time to grow. And notice the cost. Arjuna has to go alone. The brothers who have shared everything, even exile, will be apart. Yudhishthira teaches him what Vyasa taught, and Arjuna sets out, armed, toward the mountains of the north. In the epic, Draupadi speaks a blessing over him as he goes, wishing him success and asking the gods to protect him on the road. The forest has carried the Pandavas through a lot: the sun's vessel, Krishna's visit, the long arguments. Now it becomes a base camp. One brother walks out of it, and tomorrow we follow him up the mountain.
screen: `VYASA TAKES YUDHISHTHIRA ASIDE.` · `A KNOWLEDGE FOR ARJUNA.` · `SEEK THE WEAPONS OF THE GODS.` · then, large: `THE WAITING BECOMES GROWING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind some waiting in your own life, a season you can't hurry or an answer that hasn't come, and feel how it sits in you as you breathe. On each breath out, ask gently what this waiting could be for, and let the question rest there without forcing an answer. If you pray, bring that waiting into your prayer; if not, rest in the question.

782.title: Arjuna's austerities
782.hook: on the mountain, a thin old ascetic tells Arjuna to throw away his bow, and Arjuna won't
782.howItsDone: Retellings of the Mahabharata follow Arjuna to the mountain, where Indra tests him in disguise before sending him to seek Shiva; the episode is part of the long tradition of tapas, ascetic effort, in Hindu stories.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vana, the forest, became a base camp. Vyasa turned the waiting into a plan, and Arjuna set out alone. Your line was let the waiting become a plan.

Stop. The word rings out across a mountain slope in the north, and Arjuna stops. He has walked a long way, bow in hand, quiver on his back, toward a peak the epic calls Indrakila. Under a tree sits an ascetic: thin, matted hair, glowing with the strength of long discipline. He looks at the armed young man and asks, more or less: what are you doing with those? This is a place of peace. The first test of Arjuna's austerities doesn't look like a test at all.
screen: `STOP.` → `AN ASCETIC UNDER A TREE.` → `WHAT ARE YOU DOING WITH THOSE?`

segments.voice: The ascetic goes on. Here, he says, live peaceful seekers who have left anger behind. There's no need for weapons in this place. Throw away your bow. You've already reached a high state. It's a tempting offer, and he makes it again and again. But Arjuna won't put the bow down. He won't leave his brothers waiting in the forest, he says, and go off to some peaceful world without the weapons he came for. Then the ascetic shows who he really is: Indra, king of the gods, and in the story Arjuna's own father. He's pleased, and he offers his son a boon: ask for anything. Arjuna asks for weapons. Indra answers: first, you must see Shiva, the three-eyed god who holds the trident. When you've seen him, I'll give you my own weapons. So the first lesson is a surprising one. The test isn't whether he can give everything up. It's whether he knows what he came for. Indra's offer of peace sounds holy, and in another life it might be his path. But Arjuna has a purpose, a family in the forest and a promise to keep, and he holds onto it even when a radiant ascetic tells him to let it go. Austerity, here, doesn't start with fasting. It starts with being clear about why you're there.
screen: `THROW AWAY YOUR BOW.` · `ARJUNA HOLDS ON.` · `IT WAS INDRA ALL ALONG.` · then, large: `FIRST, YOU MUST SEE SHIVA.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something you're working toward right now: a task, a change, a person you're trying to show up for. Breathe in and ask why you're doing it; breathe out and let the answer be simple, and if other voices tell you to drop it, let them pass like weather on a mountain. If you pray, hold that purpose in your prayer; if not, just come back to the why.

783.title: Arjuna's austerities
783.hook: the warrior becomes an ascetic, eating less and less, until the sages of the mountain go to Shiva about him
783.howItsDone: Tapas, disciplined austerity such as fasting, stillness and self-restraint, runs through Hindu stories and practice; Arjuna on the mountain is one of the epic's pictures of a seeker whose tapas draws a god's response.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Arjuna's austerities began with a test. Indra, in disguise, told him to throw away his bow, and he wouldn't. Your line was remember why you came.

A warrior in grass clothes. That's what the sages on the mountain see when they look at the newcomer. Arjuna, prince and archer, has traded his royal dress for rags of grass and a deerskin, and taken up a staff. He's come to the foot of the Himalayas to do one thing: draw the attention of Shiva. And the way he sets about it is tapas, the slow, burning work of austerity.
screen: `A WARRIOR IN GRASS CLOTHES.` → `TO DRAW SHIVA'S ATTENTION.` → `THE BURNING WORK OF TAPAS.`

segments.voice: The epic describes it step by step. At first Arjuna eats fruit, but only every few nights. Then less often. Then less. Month by month he narrows his life, until he lives on air alone, standing on the tips of his toes with his arms raised, motionless. His hair, the text says, grows matted and bright. Now the strange part: his austerity isn't quiet. It gives off heat. In this story, tapas burns, and the burning is real. The sages who live on the mountain feel it. Smoke, in the epic's telling, seems to rise from the earth around him. Worried, they go to Shiva and say, more or less: who is this man, and what is he doing? His austerity is troubling us all. Shiva's answer is calm. Don't worry, he says. I know what's in Arjuna's heart. I know what he wants. Go back, and be at peace. So while Arjuna stands on his toes with his arms in the air, the god he came to find already knows what he's after. Arjuna hasn't said a word to Shiva. His discipline has spoken for him, loudly enough that the neighbors went to complain.
screen: `LESS FOOD, THEN ONLY AIR.` · `TAPAS GIVES OFF HEAT.` · `THE SAGES GO TO SHIVA.` · then, large: `SHIVA ALREADY KNOWS.`

segments.voice: Sit or stand still in whatever way is comfortable; there's no need to stand on your toes. 784.howItsDone: The meeting of Arjuna and Shiva as a hunter is retold in Hindu storytelling, poetry and temple art, and Shiva in the guise of a Kirata is honored as a form of the god.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Arjuna's austerities burned so hot the sages went to Shiva, and Shiva said, I know what he wants. Your line was keep discipline without announcing it.

Crashing through the trees, a boar. It's huge, and it's coming straight at Arjuna. The story tells us it's no ordinary animal: a demon named Muka has taken this shape to kill the man at prayer. Thin from fasting, Arjuna still moves fast. He grabs his bow, nocks an arrow and draws. And at that very moment, someone else is drawing too: a hunter, a Kirata, one of the mountain people, with a woman at his side and a crowd behind him. Two archers. One boar.
screen: `A BOAR CRASHES THROUGH THE TREES.` → `ARJUNA DRAWS HIS BOW.` → `SO DOES A HUNTER.`

segments.voice: The listener knows something Arjuna doesn't. The hunter is Shiva, come down the mountain in disguise, and the woman beside him is his consort Uma, also disguised. Shiva told the sages, I know what he wants. Now he's come to see what Arjuna is made of. Stop, the hunter calls. I aimed at that boar first. Arjuna ignores him and shoots. So does the hunter. Both arrows strike at the same instant, and the boar falls dead, in its own demon shape again. Arjuna is furious. Who are you, he demands, roaming this empty forest with women around you? Why did you shoot the game I had already marked? That breaks the rules of the hunt. I'll take your life for it. The hunter isn't impressed. This forest is our home, he says, more or less. I claimed that boar first. If you think you're strong, shoot. Look at the turn. In the forest, the Pandavas argued about anger and patience, about might and keeping their word. On the mountain, Arjuna held onto his purpose and burned with tapas. And now, after all that discipline, the first person he meets makes him angry in seconds. The text doesn't hide it. Arjuna's austerities have made him strong. They haven't yet made him humble. And he's about to pick a fight with the very god he came to find.
screen: `THE HUNTER IS SHIVA IN DISGUISE.` · `TWO ARROWS, ONE BOAR.` · `ARJUNA: YOU BROKE THE RULES.` · then, large: `STRONG, BUT NOT YET HUMBLE.`

As you breathe out, wonder for a moment: what if they weren't who I thought they were? You don't have to excuse anything; if you pray, you can bring that moment into your prayer.
